system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-11-11 00:24:00 to 2186-11-14 13:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation on Coumadin, dilated cardiomyopathy, systolic heart failure, diabetes, and morbid obesity was admitted for evaluation of bright red blood per rectum. He had recently lost 25 pounds due to increased diuretic therapy for heart failure. Initial workup revealed stable hemoglobin but a concerning colonic mass in the sigmoid colon. Colonoscopy and EGD showed high-grade dysplasia in the mass and gastritis, while CT scans showed no metastases. After multidisciplinary coordination and cardiac optimization, he underwent a laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy with lymph node excision. Postoperatively, he had brief episodes of hypotension and asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia, both managed conservatively. His anticoagulation was bridged with heparin, and cardiac medications were carefully resumed. He developed transient hypokalemia, which was corrected. He recovered well, tolerating a regular diet, ambulating independently, and passing stool. He was discharged home on postoperative day four with instructions to restart metolazone, monitor weight and INR, and follow up for pathology results and repeat colonoscopy in six months.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Secondary and unspecified malignant neoplasm of intra-abdominal lymph nodes
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Diabetes with ophthalmic manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Ulcer of other part of foot
Other specified disorders of circulatory system
Unspecified gastritis and gastroduodenitis, without mention of hemorrhage
Right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
Other diuretics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Anticoagulants causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old right-handed man with atrial 
fibrillation subtherapeutic on coumadin, HTN, HLD, DM2, and CHF 
who presented to the ___ ED with nausea, vomiting, posterior 
head and neck pain, and a feeling of unsteadiness on ___.

In the ED, he was given metoclopramide and ondansetron for his 
nausea. He was also noted to have left ataxia on finger to nose. 
Concerns of posterior circulation defects prompted a head CTA 
that was significant for hypoattenuation of the left medial and 
inferior cerebellar hemisphere and a diminutive left posterior 
inferior cerebellar artery, both suggestive of a left cerebellar 
infarction. The patient was then admitted to the Neurology 
Stroke service for further workup.

With concern for posterior fossa infarction, MR of the head was 
obtained which confirmed an acute to subacute left cerebellar 
infarction, but with no acute hemorrhage. The MR also revealed 
effacement of the ___ ventricle but no frank hydrocephalus. On 
exam, the patient felt symptomatically much better, but he 
became less accurate with left FNF and stood with a wide base 
and had an unsteady gait. These findings prompted a consult with 
Neurosurgery to assess for possible suboccipital craniectomy. 
Neurosurgery recommended no immediate neurosurgical 
intervention, but they favored transition to ICU for close 
neurologic monitoring, medical management and a low threshold 
for osmotic therapy. The patient was then transferred to the 
Neurology ICU.

In the Neurology ICU, the patient's INR became supratherapeutic. 
His warfarin was discontinued, and CT head was negative for any 
new swelling or hemorrhage in his brain. Otherwise, the patient 
was neurologically stable, so he was transferred back to the 
Neurology Stroke service for continued management.

His warfarin was eventually restarted for secondary stroke 
prevention given that he has atrial fibrillation. His aspirin 
was reduced from 325mg to 81mg to reduce the risk of hemorrhagic 
transformation (given that he is also taking warfarin). This 
reduction in aspirin dose was discussed with his cardiologist 
Dr. ___ who was in agreement. 

Exam improved, very mild unsteadiness on standing and taking a 
few steps, truncal ataxia improved and no appendicular ataxia. 
___ consult called for gait/balance assessment. He is very 
resistant to teaching.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,  
 
You were hospitalized due to symptoms of acute onset dizziness 
and vomiting resulting from an ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE, a 
condition where a blood vessel providing oxygen and nutrients to 
the brain is blocked by a clot. The brain is the part of your 
body that controls and directs all the other parts of your body, 
so damage to the brain from being deprived of its blood supply 
can result in a variety of symptoms.  
 
Stroke can have many different causes, so we assessed you for 
medical conditions that might raise your risk of having stroke. 
In order to prevent future strokes, we plan to modify those risk 
factors. Your risk factors are:  
- atrial fibrillation
- hypertension
- hyperlipidemia
- type II diabetes  
 
We are changing your medications as follows:  
- aspirin 81mg (from 325mg)
- please continue your coumadin and get your levels checked  
- atorvastatin 40mg po qd instead of pravastatin
 
Please take your other medications as prescribed.  
 
Please followup with Neurology and your primary care physician.  

 
If you experience any of the symptoms below, please seek 
emergency medical attention by calling Emergency Medical 
Services (dialing 911). In particular, since stroke can recur, 
please pay attention to the sudden onset and persistence of 
these symptoms:  
- sudden partial or complete loss of vision  
- sudden loss of the ability to speak words from your mouth  
- sudden loss of the ability to understand others speaking to 
you  
- sudden weakness of one side of the body  
- sudden drooping of one side of the face  
- sudden loss of sensation of one side of the body  
 
Also, please weigh yourself every morning, call your 
cardiologist if weight goes up more than 3 lbs.

Sincerely,
Your ___ Neurology Team

Home

Discharge Condition:

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,  
 
You were hospitalized due to symptoms of acute onset dizziness 
and vomiting resulting from an ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE, a 
condition where a blood vessel providing oxygen and nutrients to 
the brain is blocked by a clot. The brain is the part of your 
body that controls and directs all the other parts of your body, 
so damage to the brain from being deprived of its blood supply 
can result in a variety of symptoms.  
 
Stroke can have many different causes, so we assessed you for 
medical conditions that might raise your risk of having stroke. 
In order to prevent future strokes, we plan to modify those risk 
factors. Your risk factors are:  
- atrial fibrillation
- hypertension
- hyperlipidemia
- type II diabetes  
 
We are changing your medications as follows:  
- aspirin 81mg (from 325mg)
- please continue your coumadin and get your levels checked  
- atorvastatin 40mg po qd instead of pravastatin
 
Please take your other medications as prescribed.  
 
Please followup with Neurology and your primary care physician.  

 
If you experience any of the symptoms below, please seek 
emergency medical attention by calling Emergency Medical 
Services (dialing 911). In particular, since stroke can recur, 
please pay attention to the sudden onset and persistence of 
these symptoms:  
- sudden partial or complete loss of vision  
- sudden loss of the ability to speak words from your mouth  
- sudden loss of the ability to understand others speaking to 
you  
- sudden weakness of one side of the body  
- sudden drooping of one side of the face  
- sudden loss of sensation of one side of the body  
 
Also, please weigh yourself every morning, call your 
cardiologist if weight goes up more than 3 lbs.

Sincerely,
Your ___ Neurology Team

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the neurology doctors. You came in with nausea, vomiting, and dizziness—can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I woke up around 7:30 last night feeling really sick. I had this wave of nausea and started vomiting. At the same time, I felt like I couldn’t stand straight—like I was floating or unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you feel like the room was spinning, or was it more like you were off balance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not spinning—just unsteady. I tried to get out of bed but had to sit back down. I also got a headache in the back of my head and neck. It was tight and pounding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vision changes, slurred speech, or weakness in your arms or legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. I could talk fine, see clearly, and move my arms and legs. But I just felt too shaky to stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve given you some anti-nausea medication and fluids. Your blood sugar is high at 296, and your INR is 1.8—slightly below your target since you’re on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Coumadin for years because of my atrial fibrillation. Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it closely. Right now, we’re more concerned about the dizziness and unsteadiness. Given your symptoms, we’re worried about a possible stroke in the back of the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stroke? But I didn’t have weakness or slurred speech.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Strokes in the cerebellum—back of the brain—can cause dizziness, imbalance, and nausea without the classic symptoms. We’ve ordered a CT angiogram to check for blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the CT scan showed a possible issue in the left side of your cerebellum. To get a clearer picture, we’re going to do an MRI of your head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it definitely a stroke?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We suspect it, but the MRI will confirm. The CT showed a small area with reduced blood flow in the left cerebellum, which supplies balance and coordination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI is back. It confirms an acute to subacute stroke in the left cerebellum. There’s no bleeding, which is good, but we need to monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ve had a stroke? But I’m talking fine and thinking clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s in a part of the brain that controls balance, not speech or movement. That’s why you’re alert and talking well. But we saw some incoordination in your left hand during the exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did notice my left hand was a bit clumsy. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re admitting you to the stroke service. We’ll monitor your neurological status, manage your blood pressure, and continue your warfarin carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had two strokes before. One in the right parietal lobe, another in the temporal area. Both were related to my atrial fibrillation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows that. That’s why you’re on anticoagulants. We’ll continue warfarin for stroke prevention, but we have to be cautious with dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR came back at 4.2 this morning—higher than safe with a recent stroke. We’ve held your warfarin temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? High INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It increases bleeding risk, especially with a recent stroke. We did a head CT this morning—it shows no new bleeding or swelling. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay? No bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No bleed, and no worsening of the stroke. We’ll restart warfarin at a lower dose once your INR comes down, to keep protecting you from clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted neurosurgery because your stroke caused some swelling concern. They recommend close monitoring but no surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I thought strokes don’t need surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most don’t. But large cerebellar strokes can swell and compress the brainstem. Yours isn’t large enough for that, so we’ll manage it medically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You stood up this morning with help and took a few steps. Your balance is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel a little wobbly, especially when I turn my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The cerebellum helps with coordination. We’ve ordered outpatient physical therapy for balance and strength training.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been resistant to therapy before. But I’ll try this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. It’ll help prevent falls and improve your confidence in walking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your INR is back in range, and you’re walking with minimal help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my medications? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching you from pravastatin to atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. It’s stronger for stroke prevention. And we’re reducing your aspirin from 325 mg to 81 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower the aspirin? Isn’t more better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in your case. You’re on warfarin, so high-dose aspirin increases bleeding risk without extra protection. 81 mg is safer and still effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my insulin and heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All staying the same. Keep checking your blood sugar. We’ll also monitor your kidney function—your labs showed some acute kidney injury, likely from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking much with all the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now that you’re eating and drinking, your kidneys should recover. Just keep hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’re walking independently, no new neurological issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What should I watch for after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call 911 if you have sudden vision loss, trouble speaking, weakness on one side, facial droop, or severe imbalance. These could mean another stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my weight? My cardiologist always wants me to watch that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—weigh yourself daily. Call your cardiologist if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day. Also, keep your neurology and primary care follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel lucky this wasn’t worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re absolutely right. Catching this early and getting here quickly made a big difference. Keep up with your meds and therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your diabetes is still uncontrolled. HbA1c was 7.7. Work with your doctor on tighter control to reduce future stroke risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I need to do better with my diet and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Small steps. You’ve already taken a big one by getting care when you did. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. Stay safe and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will help you with discharge instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—physical therapy is key. It’ll help your balance and confidence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll schedule it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re on the right path.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of atrial fibrillation on warfarin, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and prior strokes presented with acute onset nausea, vomiting, posterior headache, and imbalance. MRI confirmed an acute to subacute left cerebellar infarction. He was admitted to the neurology stroke service, briefly monitored in the ICU due to supratherapeutic INR and concern for swelling, but required no surgical intervention. His warfarin was held and later restarted, and aspirin was reduced to 81 mg to minimize bleeding risk. He showed clinical improvement in coordination and gait, was able to ambulate independently, and was discharged home on day four with outpatient physical therapy, medication adjustments including a switch to atorvastatin, and close follow-up for stroke prevention and diabetes management.
